key_insight: Personalised “normative twin” cardiac models reveal hidden, reproducible patterns of heart-shape deviation that identify clinically relevant risk beyond standard measurements like ejection fraction and strain.
clinical_relevance: This approach could improve risk stratification—especially for atrial fibrillation in people with preserved ejection fraction—by spotting abnormal cardiac phenotypes that conventional biomarkers miss.
method: Built age-, sex-, and body-habitus-matched digital twins of expected healthy cardiac function.
Compared individuals against two independent shape representations: HeartSSM (128D) and MeshHeart cVAE (64D).
Derived deviation-from-norm scores and tested whether they improved prediction of outcomes beyond standard cardiac biomarkers.
evidence_signal: In UK Biobank cohorts, deviation scores improved cardiovascular risk prediction, with the strongest signal for incident atrial fibrillation in preserved-EF participants (ΔC up to +0.068; LR P = 3.3 × 10^-8), plus a smaller independent stroke signal in the MeshHeart cVAE cohort; placebo noise controls were negative.
watch_item: Generalizability and deployment need careful validation across imaging protocols and external populations, since signals varied by representation and some outcomes appeared only in one cohort/model.
paper_title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
